case_study_insert.main_stem: Bramblewick Civic Software (BCS) is a public limited company in the public-sector software (govtech) sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2013 by Yusuf Rahman, the business supplies council management and permit-processing software to local authorities across the country and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. BCS plans to invest $1,100,000 in a new AI permit-processing platform for local councils, financed by a $700,000 share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $520,000 a year, a variable cost of $95 a unit and a selling price of $135, and currently produces 22,000 units a year. BCS faces two operational problems: quality complaints about bugs in its permit module are rising and the business has a skills gap in AI and machine-learning staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 320 council procurement officers found 66% would upgrade to an AI permit-processing platform within 18 months, while 58% still use paper-based permit systems. BCS delivered 27 council contracts last year, and average permit turnaround on its current platform fell from 14 days to 6 days. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 17 per month. Net promoter score is 61. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 64 staff lack AI and machine-learning skills; off-the-job courses at the civic-tech institute cost $1,100 per employee. Staff complete on-the-job training on the permit module and off-the-job training at the civic-tech institute.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Bramblewick Civic Software for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% from $13.30 to $13.94 per hour from April 2026. (3) Local council IT budgets are capped at a 2.0% increase next year, while council pay and energy costs are forecast to rise 6.5% and inflation is running at 6.1%, squeezing discretionary software spending.

questions.question_text: BCS plans to raise $700,000 of its $1,100,000 expansion through a share issue. Explain two advantages for BCS of using a share issue rather than a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no fixed repayment schedule and no interest, so BCS avoids adding heavy debt-service costs on top of fixed costs of $520,000 a year. The AI permit-processing platform will take time to generate revenue from the 66% of 320 surveyed council procurement officers willing to upgrade within 18 months; equity financing lets BCS fund that ramp-up without breaching cash reserves or missing council service-level commitments.

Point 2: Selling shares to a wider investor base spreads the risk of an ambitious $1,100,000 public-sector technology project across many shareholders rather than concentrating it on BCS and its retained profit alone. As a public limited company, BCS can also use the issue to raise its profile with council clients and future investors, and the permanent capital strengthens the balance sheet — reflected in capital employed of $11,400,000 — supporting further contracts without granting any lender security over the platform or diluting control in the same way debt covenants might restrict autocratic decision-making.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Bramblewick Civic Software and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: BCS is launching its AI permit-processing platform to local councils. Consider a free 90-day pilot for the first 10 councils, a case-study feature in the Local Government Chronicle trade press, or targeted LinkedIn advertising to council procurement officers. Which should BCS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Free 90-day pilot for the first 10 councils: A free pilot lets councils test the AI permit-processing platform on real applications, directly demonstrating the fall in turnaround from 14 days to 6 days BCS achieved on its current platform. Councils are risk-averse public bodies, and a no-cost trial lowers the barrier to change for the 58% still using paper-based permit systems. Risks are that the pilot is not free for BCS — it consumes support capacity from a 64-person team — and unsuccessful deployments could publicly sour future procurement, but converting even a few pilots into contracts validates the whole $1,100,000 investment.

Local Government Chronicle case-study feature: A trade-press feature builds credibility with councillors and procurement officers nationwide and positions Yusuf Rahman as a thought leader. Print coverage is cheap and enduring, but it is passive: procurement cycles are long, officers rarely buy directly from an article, and measurable lead generation is weak compared with hands-on proof.

Targeted LinkedIn advertising: LinkedIn advertising can reach the exact procurement officers whose attitudes BCS measured — 66% of 320 officers willing to upgrade within 18 months — with measurable click-through and retargeting. However, busy officers are wary of unsolicited adverts, public-sector procurement usually requires formal tenders and due diligence rather than advert-driven impulse, and ad spend is wasted on officers whose councils lack the budget headroom created by the 2.0% IT budget cap.

Recommendation: BCS should choose the free 90-day pilot. It converts the platform's strongest proof point — 14-day to 6-day permit turnaround — into signed council contracts, engaging the 58% paper-based holdouts directly and generating case-study evidence for every later campaign. The trade-press feature is rejected as too passive to drive tenders, and LinkedIn advertising is rejected as spray-and-pray against a capped-budget, compliance-driven public-sector buyer that needs hands-on, risk-free evidence first.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BCS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BCS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the trade-press feature and LinkedIn advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: BCS operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for BCS of its hierarchical structure when delivering council contracts.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives BCS clear lines of responsibility from Yusuf Rahman down through team leads to developers, testers and council-liaison staff, which is essential in regulated public-sector delivery. Audit trails for permit decisions, data-handling approvals and quality sign-offs are unambiguous — one named manager owns each stage — directly reducing the quality complaints about bugs in the permit module and supporting the supermarket-style service reviews council clients expect.

Point 2: Defined roles and a narrow span of control let BCS run specialised units — core development, council liaison, support and AI research — each with clear accountability for its own output. This supports consistent, repeatable delivery across its 27 council contracts and makes it easier to spot where in the 64-person workforce the AI skills gap sits, so training at $1,100 per employee from the civic-tech institute can be targeted at the right layer rather than spread thinly, protecting margins in a market where council IT budgets are capped at a 2.0% rise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to BCS's structure and council delivery.

questions.question_text: BCS must close an AI and machine-learning skills gap among 18 staff. Consider on-the-job training shadowing its AI engineers or off-the-job training at the civic-tech institute. Which should BCS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training shadowing AI engineers: Shadowing lets the 18 staff learn on live permit-processing code and real council data, which is the fastest way to make them productive on the $1,100,000 AI platform. It avoids the $19,800 course fee (18 staff at $1,100) and keeps the council service running. Drawbacks are that BCS's scarce AI engineers — already overloaded by the skills gap — lose productive hours mentoring, knowledge transfer is informal and uncertified, and shadowing alone will not give the structured grounding needed to reduce quality complaints about bugs, which have only fallen from 33 to 17 per month.

Off-the-job training at the civic-tech institute: The institute course gives the 18 staff a recognised, structured AI and machine-learning curriculum with external assessment — valuable when councils demand evidence of competence and audit-ready processes. The $19,800 cost is modest against the $1,100,000 expansion and against BCS's revenue of $11,400,000. The drawbacks are time away from 27 live council contracts, and the course content is generic rather than tuned to BCS's permit module, so on-site application afterwards is still needed.

Decision: BCS should choose off-the-job training at the civic-tech institute. The quality complaints and rising complexity of the AI platform demand systematic, certified skills rather than ad-hoc shadowing for regulated public-sector work; the $19,800 fee is easily affordable and councils will trust accredited competence. On-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because it overburdens BCS's few AI engineers, delivers no external certification for audits, and previously coexisted with the current skills gap; shadowing can supplement the course for two weeks afterwards to apply the learning to live permits.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of BCS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of BCS with a well-justified decision covering cost, auditability and workload.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BCS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $520,000 ÷ ($135 − $95) = $520,000 ÷ $40 = 13,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 13,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $135 − $95 = $40. Answer: contribution per unit is $40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BCS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 13,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 22,000 units to confirm a healthy margin of safety of 9,000 units, giving confidence that the $1,100,000 AI platform can be funded while retaining cover against contract delays or tender losses.
2. Contribution per unit of $40 lets managers test promotional pricing for the free 90-day pilot-to-contract conversion, for example modelling whether discounted first-year licences still cover the $95 variable cost, before approaching the 58% of paper-based councils.
3. Fixed costs of $520,000 a year and the $40 contribution can be used to model how quickly the $700,000 share issue funds are recovered as the 66% of officers willing to upgrade sign contracts, and to set licence-volume targets for the autocratic leadership team.
4. Unit-cost data ($520,000 ÷ 22,000 units + $95 = $118.64 a unit) lets managers benchmark licence costs, identify where bug-fixing and the 17 monthly complaints inflate delivery effort, and redirect resources to the AI skills gap to drive complaints toward zero.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 13,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $40 | (iii) Four contextual uses: the 9,000-unit margin of safety against 22,000 units confirms headroom; contribution per unit of $40 supports pilot and discount modelling; fixed costs of $520,000 are tested against the $700,000 share issue; and unit costs of $118.64 are benchmarked to attack quality complaints and the AI skills gap.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BCS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BCS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 60.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 60.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 22.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue grew from $9,600,000 in 2024 to $11,400,000 in 2025, a rise of 18.75%. Cost of sales rose proportionally from $3,840,000 to $4,560,000, holding gross profit growth in line with revenue and lifting gross profit from $5,760,000 to $6,840,000. Operating profit increased from $1,920,000 to $2,508,000, up 30.6%, a faster rate than revenue — evidence of genuine scale efficiency and tight control of fixed costs at $520,000 a year. Capital employed rose from $9,600,000 to $11,400,000, exactly in line with revenue growth, while interest payable climbed from $140,000 to $165,000.

Evaluation: Operating performance has improved even though the top-line conversion of revenue into gross profit stayed flat at 60.0%. The operating improvement from 20.0% to 22.0% shows BCS converting extra revenue into profit efficiently, and the return on capital employed confirms the larger asset base is working harder, not idle. The unchanged 60.0% gross figure suggests limited scope to raise licence prices further given council IT budgets are capped at a 2.0% increase; future margin gains must come from AI automation reducing delivery cost per permit. Residual risks: interest payable is rising, quality complaints cost engineer time, and the 2.0% council budget cap could stall upgrade deals.

Conclusion: BCS's financial performance has improved. Operating profit grew faster than revenue and capital employed, the flat gross conversion was held at a healthy 60.0%, and the return on capital employed rose from 20.0% to 22.0%. The improvement is real but narrow — BCS must now deliver AI-driven cost savings to protect margins against the budget cap.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue growth, cost proportionality, capital employed and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether BCS's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BCS of launching a citizen-facing mobile app that lets residents report issues such as potholes and missed waste collections.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A citizen app extends BCS's platform from council back offices into residents' pockets, creating an end-to-end product that councils find far harder to displace once deployed. The richer data stream — geo-tagged reports, photos and categories — would strengthen BCS's AI models, raise switching costs, and open a new recurring fee stream on top of the 27 council contracts, accelerating adoption among the 66% of procurement officers already willing to upgrade within 18 months and lifting BCS's case for the $700,000 share issue.

Disadvantage: The app would divert scarce AI and mobile-development capacity from the permit platform at exactly the moment the business already faces a skills gap of 18 staff, risking delay to the $1,100,000 launch and more quality complaints instead of fewer. It also creates ongoing maintenance, accessibility and data-protection obligations — councils will hold BCS to account for residents' personal data — stretching a 64-person team and raising fixed costs above $520,000 a year before revenue arrives.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BCS's platform, skills gap and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise from 4.25% to 4.75%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the cap of 2.0% on council IT budgets will affect BCS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.75%): BCS is financing its $1,100,000 expansion through a $700,000 share issue and $400,000 retained profit, so it has no new variable-rate loan and the direct extra interest cost is limited to the modest interest payable of $140,000 to $165,000 on existing borrowing. The indirect effect is that councils themselves face higher borrowing costs and may delay capital projects, and BCS's own future loan capacity for phase two narrows. Manageable, but worth watching.

Minimum wage increase (4.8%, from $13.30 to $13.94 per hour): With 64 staff, mainly developers, liaison officers and support staff, BCS will feel the 4.8% rise mainly among junior and support roles near the minimum wage. If 24 staff sit near $13.30 an hour, the annual base is roughly 24 staff × 2,000 hours × $13.30 = $638,400, so the rise adds roughly $30,600 a year — meaningful but not decisive against $2,508,000 of operating profit, and partly offset by productivity from the AI platform.

Council IT budget cap (2.0% maximum increase next year): This is a demand-side shock aimed directly at BCS's customer base. With council pay and energy costs forecast to rise 6.5%, discretionary software spend is the squeeze target: new AI permit-processing licences risk being deferred or shrunk even though 66% of 320 surveyed officers want to upgrade. The cap also pressures renewal pricing across the 27 live council contracts, threatening BCS's 18.75% revenue growth and the case for its $700,000 share issue.

Conclusion: The 2.0% cap on council IT budgets will have the greatest impact. BCS sells almost entirely into councils, so capping their discretionary technology spend directly suppresses BCS's sales pipeline, renewal uplift and expansion case, whereas the wage rise adds only about $30,600 a year and the interest-rate move barely touches an equity-financed balance sheet. BCS must respond with hard ROI evidence — the 14-day to 6-day permit turnaround and measurable savings — to win scarce budget within the cap.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BCS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BCS with a well-justified judgement that the council IT budget cap has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
